editor_spans.body: The Motherwell speech is best read as a diagnosis of where power sits rather than a policy offer. Burnham's own account of Ravenscraig and the Leigh coalfield puts the damage down to decisions taken far away by people who never lived with the consequences. His remedy is structural: push power below the national level, whether that level is Westminster or Holyrood. That is why he treats the 1999 settlement as unfinished rather than complete.

There is an irony in the method. The model he holds up, Easterhouse's 'names not numbers' approach, was born in Glasgow, not Manchester. He carried it south and is now offering it back to Scotland as a nationwide template. Scotland was not short of the idea. What it lacked, on his own telling, was an institutional route for a one-estate project to become the way every jobseeker is treated. That makes the DWP devolution offer the one concrete lever in the speech, because employment support is where a centrally designed, tick-box system meets people directly.

The tension is that a bottom-up philosophy is arriving with a top-down clock. Downing Street wants a new model designed 'in the immediate months ahead'. It calls Holyrood's own local government reform too slow. It warns that Scottish towns will be left 'underpowered' while northern English cities 'power up'. To an SNP government, that comparison reads less as an invitation than as competitive pressure. A Prime Minister arguing against the centre is setting the pace and the terms from the centre.

The scale also deserves a sober look against the problems he names. On one side sit a seven-year life expectancy gap across ten miles, one in six young people not in education, employment or training, and high streets one-fifth empty in Dundee. On the other sit the tangible items: £10 million matched for two colleges, a billion pounds of research money spread across the whole UK, and a National Economic Council meeting the devolved leaders for the first time under this government. Those gaps were built over decades of deindustrialisation. Changing who decides is necessary, but devolved power without devolved money tends to hand local leaders responsibility for decline rather than the means to reverse it. The real test will be what budgets, not just functions, cross the border and then go down to the regions.
